title: A folder that remembers
subtitle: Ravi gets a new version every week; Maya puts the files in a vault, shares the read key once, and every version stays. 9 panels.
rule: Every line a character says is the storyboard's, not a quote, and is marked not_a_quote; evidence panels quote this site's pages word for word, which the build checks.

scenes.title: A folder that remembers
scenes.subtitle: Files in a vault: versioned, updatable, shared once.
scenes.note: The second thing the brief asked for: files kept in vaults, not one-shot transfers.

scenes.caption: Which one is current?

cast.says: Every week a new link. Which one is current?

scenes.note: The problem a transfer cannot solve: there is no second version of a transfer.

scenes.caption: Into a vault instead

cast.says: Into a vault. One place, every version.

scenes.note: A vault is a folder of files, encrypted here, versioned like git.

scenes.caption: Every change is a commit
scenes.note: Each write is one commit with a message; two devices merge with compare-and-swap.

scenes.caption: Two keys

cast.says: The read key is the one I share.

scenes.note: The read key is derived one way from the vault key; it can never become write access.

scenes.caption: Ravi always sees the latest
scenes.note: The read-key link opens every file and every version, read only.

scenes.caption: And on a laptop
scenes.note: The browser and the CLI are two clones of one vault.

scenes.caption: Why the read key can be shared

evidence.quote: The read key is derived from the vault key one way, so a read key can never be turned back into write access.

scenes.note: Quoted from the vaults and keys page, word for word.

scenes.punchline: Share the read key once. Keep the vault key. Every version stays.
scenes.note: Create, add, publish, open by read key: driven by the browser test.
